notes.definition: Feeding relationships within a community can be represented by food chains, which always begin with a producer. Ecologists use quadrats and transects to measure the abundance and distribution of species in an ecosystem.
explanation: Feeding relationships within a community can be shown as food chains. All food chains begin with a producer, which synthesises molecules (makes its own food). This is usually a green plant or alga, which makes glucose by photosynthesis using light energy. Producers are eaten by primary consumers (herbivores). Primary consumers may be eaten by secondary consumers, and secondary consumers by tertiary consumers. The arrows in a food chain show the direction in which biomass and energy are transferred, so they point from the organism being eaten to the organism that eats it.

Consumers that kill and eat other animals are called predators, and the animals they eat are called prey. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. When prey numbers increase there is more food for predators, so more predators survive and breed and the predator population increases. More predators eat more prey, so the prey population falls. With less food the predator population then falls, which allows the prey to increase again. On a graph the predator peak comes after the prey peak, and predator numbers are usually lower.

Ecologists measure the abundance (how many there are) and the distribution (where they are found) of species using sampling. It is usually impossible to count every organism in a large area, so they count organisms in small sample areas and scale up. A quadrat is a square frame, often 0.25 m² (50 cm × 50 cm) or 1 m², placed on the ground. The number of a species inside the quadrat is counted, or its percentage cover is estimated.

To estimate population size, quadrats are placed at random so that the sample is representative and not biased by where the investigator chooses to look. One method is to lay two tape measures at right angles along the edges of the area and use a random number generator to give coordinates. After counting many quadrats, calculate the mean number per quadrat. Then: estimated population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat). More quadrats give a more representative result.

To investigate how a factor affects distribution, a transect is used. A tape measure is laid out in a line across a habitat where conditions change, such as from the shade of a tree into an open field, or from a pond edge up a bank. Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the line (for example every 2 m), and the number or percentage cover of a species is recorded at each point, along with an abiotic factor such as light intensity or soil moisture. This shows how the distribution of a species changes with the factor.

You need to understand mean, median and mode for field data. The mean is the total divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value when the data are placed in order (if there are two middle values, find the halfway point between them). The mode is the most common value. You should also be able to plot suitable graphs with sensible scales, for example a bar chart of mean number per quadrat at different sites, or a line or scatter graph of number against distance along a transect.
keyFacts: All food chains begin with a producer: usually a green plant or alga that makes glucose by photosynthesis.
Producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer.
Arrows in a food chain show the direction of energy and biomass transfer (from eaten to eater).
Predators kill and eat other animals; prey are the animals eaten.
In a stable community predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles, with the predator peak lagging behind the prey peak.
Quadrats placed at random are used to estimate population size.
Estimated population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area).
Transects with quadrats at regular intervals show how distribution changes with an abiotic factor.
Mean = total ÷ number of values; median = middle value in order; mode = most common value.
Required practical 9: measure population size of a common species and investigate the effect of a factor on its distribution.

keyTerms.definition: An organism that synthesises its own food molecules, usually a green plant or alga making glucose by photosynthesis; the start of every food chain.
An organism that eats producers (a herbivore).
An organism that eats primary consumers.
An organism that eats secondary consumers.
A consumer that kills and eats other animals.
A square frame of known area used to sample organisms in a habitat.
A line (often a tape measure) across a habitat along which samples are taken at regular intervals to study distribution.
The number of individuals of a species in an area.
Where organisms of a species are found within a habitat.
Choosing sample positions without bias, for example using random coordinates, so the results are representative.

equations.name: Estimating population size
equations.formula: estimated population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)
equations.units: number of organisms (areas in the same units, for example m²)

equations.name: Mean
equations.formula: mean = sum of values ÷ number of values

workedExamples.title: Calculating a mean number per quadrat
workedExamples.question: A student counted dandelions in 8 quadrats: 3, 5, 0, 4, 6, 2, 5, 7. Calculate the mean, median and mode.
steps: Order the values: 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7. There are two middle values (4 and 5), so median = (4 + 5) ÷ 2 = 4.5.
Mode: 5 appears twice, more than any other value, so the mode is 5.
workedExamples.answer: Mean = 4, median = 4.5, mode = 5 dandelions per quadrat.

workedExamples.title: Scaling up to estimate population size
workedExamples.question: A field measures 40 m × 25 m. Using 0.25 m² quadrats placed at random, the mean number of daisies is 6 per quadrat. Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
steps: Number of quadrats that would fit = 1000 ÷ 0.25 = 4000.
Check another way: 6 per 0.25 m² = 24 per m²; 24 × 1000 = 24 000.

workedExamples.title: Converting quadrat size units
workedExamples.question: A quadrat has sides of 50 cm. Twelve quadrats contained a total of 72 clover plants. The lawn is 300 m². Estimate the clover population.
steps: Convert: 50 cm = 0.5 m, so quadrat area = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m².

misconceptions.wrong: Students often draw food chain arrows pointing from the eater to the food ('the fox eats the rabbit').
misconceptions.right: In fact arrows show the direction of energy and biomass transfer, so they point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it: rabbit → fox.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the predator population peaks at the same time as the prey.
misconceptions.right: In fact the predator peak lags behind, because predators take time to reproduce after their food supply increases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think placing quadrats where there are lots of plants gives a better result.
misconceptions.right: In fact quadrats must be placed at random to avoid bias; choosing positions makes the sample unrepresentative.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often multiply the mean per quadrat by the field area without allowing for the quadrat size.
misconceptions.right: In fact you multiply by total area ÷ quadrat area. If the quadrat is 0.25 m², first convert to number per m² (× 4).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a transect is used to estimate population size.
misconceptions.right: In fact random quadrats estimate population size; a transect shows how distribution changes across a habitat with an abiotic factor.

realWorld: Conservation scientists use quadrat surveys to monitor rare plants such as orchids and to decide whether protection measures are working.
Transects across sand dunes and salt marshes show how plant communities change with distance from the sea, helping coastal management.
Long-term records of lynx and snowshoe hare furs collected by trading companies in Canada provided the classic evidence of predator-prey cycles.
examTips: Draw food chain arrows from food to feeder (in the direction of energy transfer). Start every food chain with a producer.
For population estimates, write the steps: mean per quadrat, convert to number per m² if needed, then multiply by total area. Check the area units match.
To explain why quadrats are placed randomly, say 'to avoid bias' and 'so the sample is representative'. To improve reliability, say 'use more quadrats'.
For predator-prey graphs, describe the lag and explain it: prey increase, so more food, so predators increase later; then more prey are eaten.
Know the difference: random quadrats for abundance (population size); transects for distribution linked to a changing factor.
summary: Food chains start with a producer (green plant or alga) that makes glucose by photosynthesis.
Producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer.
Predator and prey populations cycle, with predator peaks after prey peaks.
Random quadrats estimate population size: mean per quadrat × total area ÷ quadrat area.
Transects show how distribution changes with an abiotic factor.
Mean, median and mode summarise sample data; more samples give more representative results.

markScheme: 1 mark: primary consumer
questions.explanation: The rabbit eats the producer (grass), so it is the primary consumer. The fox is the secondary consumer.

questions.question: What do the arrows in a food chain represent?
options: The direction of energy and biomass transfer
The direction in which animals move
Which organism eats the other, pointing towards the food
markScheme: 1 mark: the direction of energy and biomass transfer
questions.explanation: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the organism eating it, showing energy and biomass moving along the chain. Pointing towards the food is the common reversed mistake.

questions.question: Which piece of equipment is a square frame used to sample plants in a field?
markScheme: 1 mark: quadrat
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a square frame of known area. A pooter and pitfall trap catch small animals, and a light meter measures light intensity.

questions.question: Why should quadrats be placed at random when estimating the population of a plant in a field?
options: To make sure every quadrat contains the plant
To avoid bias so the sample is representative
So that the quadrats do not overlap the transect
markScheme: 1 mark: to avoid bias so the sample is representative
questions.explanation: If the investigator chooses where to put quadrats they may pick areas with more plants, biasing the estimate. Random placement gives a fair sample.

questions.question: A student wants to find out how the number of a moss species changes from the edge of a wood into the middle. Which method is most suitable?
options: Placing quadrats at random across the whole wood
Counting all the moss plants in one quadrat
Placing quadrats at regular intervals along a transect
Using a pitfall trap at the edge of the wood
markScheme: 1 mark: placing quadrats at regular intervals along a transect
questions.explanation: A transect samples along a line where conditions change, showing how distribution changes. Random quadrats are for estimating total population size.

questions.question:
A student counted the number of buttercups in 7 quadrats.
Table 1 shows the results.
What is the mode?
markScheme: 1 mark: 5
questions.explanation: The mode is the most common value: 5 appears three times. The mean is 29 ÷ 7 = 4.1, and 7 is the range (8 − 1), not the mode.

options: Predator numbers are high so more prey are eaten
Predator numbers have fallen, so fewer prey are eaten
Prey numbers are high so there is more competition for food
Predators have started to eat producers instead
markScheme: 1 mark: predator numbers have fallen, so fewer prey are eaten
questions.explanation: Prey increase when predator numbers are low, because fewer are killed and more survive to breed. High predator numbers would cause prey to fall.

questions.question: A student estimates the population of daisies in a field using only 3 quadrats. Which change would make the estimate most representative of the whole field?
options: Using 3 larger quadrats placed where daisies are common
Counting the daisies in the same 3 quadrats twice
Using a transect from one corner
markScheme: 1 mark: using 20 quadrats placed at random
questions.explanation: A larger random sample better represents variation across the field. Choosing where daisies are common adds bias, and recounting the same quadrats does not sample more of the field.

questions.question: Which organism is most likely to be a producer?
markScheme: 1 mark: seaweed (alga)
questions.explanation: Algae photosynthesise, so they are producers. Mushrooms are fungi (decomposers), and earthworms and snails are consumers.

1 mark: (b) stickleback
questions.explanation: Algae are the producer, water fleas the primary consumer, sticklebacks the secondary consumer and pike the tertiary consumer.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by a producer.
markScheme: 1 mark: an organism that makes (synthesises) its own food molecules
1 mark: by photosynthesis (for example a green plant or alga making glucose)
questions.explanation: Producers capture light energy and make glucose, which provides biomass for the rest of the food chain.

questions.question: Describe how a student could use random sampling to place quadrats in a field.
acceptedAnswers: two tape measures at right angles
markScheme: 1 mark: lay out two tape measures at right angles along two edges of the field to form axes
1 mark: use a random number generator (or table) to generate coordinates
1 mark: place the quadrat at each coordinate and repeat for a large number of quadrats (for example 10 or more)
questions.explanation: Coordinates generated randomly remove the investigator's choice, avoiding bias. Using many quadrats makes the sample more representative.

questions.question: When using quadrats, the student must decide whether to count plants that are partly inside the quadrat. Suggest a rule they could use and explain why a rule is needed.
acceptedAnswers: count if more than half inside
count plants touching two sides only
markScheme: 1 mark: a sensible rule, for example count a plant only if more than half of it is inside, or count those touching the top and left edges but not the other two
1 mark: so counting is consistent between quadrats / results are comparable
questions.explanation: Without a clear rule, borderline plants may be counted differently each time, reducing the reliability and comparability of the data.

questions.question: A transect was laid from a hedge into an open field. Name one abiotic factor the student could measure at each quadrat and the equipment they could use.
acceptedAnswers: soil pH and pH probe or indicator
markScheme: 1 mark: an abiotic factor (light intensity, temperature, soil moisture, soil pH)
1 mark: matching equipment (light meter, thermometer or temperature probe, moisture meter, pH probe or soil test kit)
questions.explanation: Measuring an abiotic factor at each point lets you look for a correlation between the factor and the distribution of the species.

questions.question:
A student placed quadrats at intervals along a transect from under the trees at the edge of a wood into an open field.
Table 1 shows the results.
The student concluded that ferns grow better in low light.
Give two reasons why this conclusion may not be valid and suggest one improvement.
markScheme: 1 mark: other factors (for example soil moisture, temperature, soil pH) may also change along the transect
1 mark: only one transect / few quadrats so data may not be representative / correlation does not prove causation
1 mark: improvement: repeat with several transects, or measure other abiotic factors at each quadrat
questions.explanation: Field data show correlation. Shade from trees also changes moisture and temperature, so the cause cannot be identified from one transect alone.

acceptedAnswers: predators eat prey so prey fall
markScheme: 1 mark: when prey increase there is more food for predators
1 mark: so more predators survive and reproduce
1 mark: reproduction (and growth of young) takes time, so the predator increase lags behind / the predator peak is reached when prey are already falling
questions.explanation: The key word is 'lag': predator numbers respond to food supply only after a breeding delay.

questions.question: Name the type of consumer that eats a primary consumer.
markScheme: 1 mark: secondary consumer
questions.explanation: Secondary consumers eat primary consumers; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.

questions.question:
A student counted the number of daisies in five quadrats.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.
questions.explanation: Add the values (3 + 5 + 2 + 6 + 4 = 20) and divide by the number of quadrats (5): mean = 4.

questions.question:
A student counted the number of dandelions in six quadrats.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the median number of dandelions per quadrat.
markScheme: 1 mark: values in order: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8
1 mark: median = (3 + 5) ÷ 2 = 4
questions.explanation: Put the values in order first: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values, 3 and 5, so it is 4. Taking the middle of the unordered list (8 and 3) would wrongly give 5.5.

questions.question: A school field measures 120 m × 80 m. A student placed ten 1 m² quadrats at random and counted 85 clover plants in total. Estimate the number of clover plants in the field.
markScheme: 1 mark: mean = 85 ÷ 10 = 8.5 per m²
1 mark: field area = 120 × 80 = 9600 m²
questions.explanation: Mean per quadrat (8.5) × number of 1 m² quadrats that fit in the field (9600) = 81 600 plants.

questions.question: A quadrat of area 0.25 m² contained a mean of 6 thistles. Calculate the mean number of thistles per m².
questions.answerLabel: Mean number of thistles per m²
markScheme: 1 mark: 24 per m²
questions.explanation: Four 0.25 m² quadrats fit in 1 m², so multiply by 4: 6 × 4 = 24 per m². Multiplying by 0.25 (giving 1.5) is a common error.

questions.question: A student used 20 quadrats, each 50 cm × 50 cm, and counted 140 buttercups in total. The meadow has an area of 0.5 hectares (1 hectare = 10 000 m²). Estimate the buttercup population of the meadow.
markScheme: 1 mark: mean = 140 ÷ 20 = 7 per quadrat; quadrat area = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m²
1 mark: 7 ÷ 0.25 = 28 per m²; meadow area = 0.5 × 10 000 = 5000 m²
questions.explanation: Convert everything to m²: quadrat 0.25 m², meadow 5000 m². Mean 7 per quadrat is 28 per m², and 28 × 5000 = 140 000. Forgetting to convert 50 cm to 0.5 m gives a wildly wrong answer.

questions.question:
A rectangular lawn measures 15 m × 12 m.
A student placed 0.25 m² quadrats at random on the lawn.
Table 1 shows the number of daisies in each quadrat.
Estimate the daisy population of the lawn.
markScheme: 1 mark: mean = 36 ÷ 8 = 4.5 per quadrat
1 mark: number of quadrats in lawn = (15 × 12) ÷ 0.25 = 180 ÷ 0.25 = 720
questions.explanation: Total = 36, mean = 4.5 per 0.25 m² (18 per m²). Lawn area 180 m². 18 × 180 = 3240. The two routes (×720 quadrats, or ×4 then ×180 m²) give the same answer.

questions.question: Required practical: describe a method a student could use to estimate the population size of daisies on a school field. Include how they would calculate their estimate.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure the length and width of the field to find its area; lay two tape measures at right angles to form axes; use a random number generator to give coordinates; place a quadrat (for example 0.25 m² or 1 m²) at the coordinates; count the number of daisies inside the quadrat; use a rule for daisies on the edge; repeat for a large number of quadrats (for example at least 10 to 20); calculate the mean number per quadrat; estimated population = mean per quadrat × (field area ÷ quadrat area); more quadrats give a more representative estimate.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logically ordered method including random placement with a valid technique, counting, repeats, and the correct scaling calculation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method including quadrats and counting with either random placement or the calculation described.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements such as 'use a quadrat and count the daisies'.
questions.explanation: Top answers cover: how to place quadrats randomly, what to count, how many repeats, and the scaling-up calculation with matching area units.

questions.question: Required practical: a student wants to investigate how the distribution of a plant species changes with light intensity, from under a large tree out into an open field. Describe a method the student could use and explain how they would make the results valid.
markScheme: Indicative content: lay a tape measure (transect) from the base of the tree out into the open field; place a quadrat at regular intervals along the line (for example every 1 m or 2 m); count the number of plants or estimate percentage cover in each quadrat; measure light intensity at each quadrat with a light meter, held at the same height and at the same time of day; repeat the transect several times in different directions or on different days and calculate means; keep other variables the same where possible (same quadrat size, same counting rule, same time of day, similar weather); also measure other abiotic factors such as soil moisture to check whether they also change; plot number of plants (or mean) against light intensity or distance; look for a correlation.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed transect method with regular sampling, measurement of light intensity, repeats and controls, and recognition that other factors may vary.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a transect method with sampling and light measurement, with some reference to repeats or control.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple reference to quadrats or a tape measure without a clear method.
questions.explanation: Distribution with a changing factor needs a transect, not random quadrats. Validity comes from controlling what you can (time of day, quadrat size, counting rule) and repeating the transect.

questions.question: In a forest, owls are predators of mice. Describe and explain how the populations of owls and mice would be expected to change over several years in a stable community.
markScheme: Indicative content: both populations rise and fall in cycles; mouse numbers rise first; more mice means more food for owls; more owls survive and breed so the owl population rises (after a delay); more owls eat more mice so mouse numbers fall; with less food owl numbers then fall; fewer owls allows mice to increase again; owl numbers are lower than mouse numbers; owl peaks lag behind mouse peaks.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the cyclical pattern including the lag and explains the link between food supply and predation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that populations go up and down or that owls eat mice, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: Describe (cycles, lag) and explain (food supply drives predator numbers; predation drives prey numbers).
